content.text: , Can you provide a sample of the type of RDF you are ingesting?
Andrew-
Here's a sample of the RDF/XML I'm posting.  Before posting, the ingest tool checks whether each described Fedora URIs exists, and creates it if necessary.
Early testing of the migration-utils seems to run up against this as well...
https://github.com/fcrepo4-labs/migration-utils/issues/18
, is it safe to assume this ticket is not currently "In Progress"?
Just to add, we've seen this too with an ingest of about 2000 fairly small objects (metadata only) via Hydra AF9. We thought it might be solvable with better tomcat / jvm tuning but perhaps not.
The Fedora 4.2, running on Tomcat 8.0.12, jdk1.8.0_45, with JAVA_OPTS = -Xms3g -Xmx3g, after ingesting
about 70,000 Fedora Objects and 400,000 Datastream, is running out of memory and the server is not responding.
Resources for tuning GC to help debug this issue:
https://confluence.atlassian.com/display/CONFKB/Confluence+crashes+due+to+java.lang.OutOfMemoryError+GC+overhead+limit+exceeded
https://confluence.atlassian.com/display/CONFKB/Enable+Garbage+Collection+Logging
https://confluence.atlassian.com/display/ENTERPRISE/Garbage+Collection+%28GC%29+Tuning+Guide
https://github.com/chewiebug/GCViewer
http://tech.shift.com/post/74311817513/cassandra-tuning-the-jvm-for-read-heavy-workloads
, can you provide a link to one or two example documents which you are trying to ingest when you hit this error?
It was a batch process reading an XML and creating 2000 relatively simple objects, see code snippet below. Problem here more to do with
speed
of creation than quantity of data, I think:
h = Concept.new
h.rdftype += ['http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#Concept', 'http://fedora.info/definitions/v4/indexing#Indexable']
h.preflabel = i.css('skos|prefLabel').text
h.concept_scheme = @scheme
if i.css('skos|altLabel')
i.css('skos|altLabel').each do |i|
h.altlabel += [i.text]
end
end
if i.css('skos|definition').text != ''
h.definition = i.css('skos|definition').text
end
h.save
if i.css('skos|broader').text == ''
h.istopconcept = 'true'
@scheme.topconcept += [h]
@scheme.save
end
h.identifier = h.id
h.former_id = i.values
h.save
, thanks. Can you also share your JAVA_OPTS settings?
For the record, with the:
following command
for x in {0..50000}; do echo "number $x"; echo ""; curl -i -XPOST -H"Content-Type: text/turtle" --data-binary @body.rdf localhost:8080/fcrepo/rest; done
attached `body.rdf`
default JAVA_OPTS (meaning no additional configuration)
I hit a GC OOM at 3430 requests.
I saw it consistently with default settings, Paul (my dev) has seen it intermittently with these settings:
CATALINA_OPTS="$CATALINA_OPTS -server -Xmx512m -Xmx1024m"
it happens more often if Fedora/tomcat have been in use for a few hours before running the task, as if there is a build up of memory use
We've also seen this error:
ERROR 18:25:37.924 (InvocationContextInterceptor) ISPN000136: Execution error
java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space
It’s a bug only if Fedora is making a guarantee that even when there are long running ingests, it will work within a specific heap range.

The OOM stacktrace is really a warning by the JVM that the code is inefficient for three things: (a) a memory setting; (b) a data set (I used the ticket’s 6K RDF file, I’m assuming that’s a representative sample); (c) a particular system (I tested it on a desktop Windows  machine with Tomcat 8 on a standard electro-mechanical disk).

After successfully running various tests for 160 hours and ingesting, without restart, about 350K items (using Andrew’s command and data) and finding out that the heap usage actually decreases with time, I’m not sure if the ticket (and the experience) should be classified as a bug.

I ran the ingest on a Windows desktop machine (the defaults on my machine are: Java 8 Hotspot Server VM, 4-8GB memory (it used around 3 GB), parallel garbage collector) and did not run into any relevant issues. Initially, the heap usage was a bit high but it settled down to about 1.7 GB. The ratio of GC activity was pretty reasonable throughout my tests, hence there was little possibility of a GC Out of Memory error. I can share a screenshot, if somebody is interested.
The JVM documentation says the following:

Both parallel and collector will “ will throw an OutOfMemoryError if too much time is being spent in garbage collection: if more than 98% of the total time is spent in garbage collection and less than 2% of the heap is recovered, an OutOfMemoryError will be thrown”.

Of course, we could look at the source code to make Fedora use less heap and thus make it spend less time garbage collecting, but I think a different ticket regarding performance-tuning should be created as there is no guarantee that users would not see this stack trace even when the modifications have been made (let’s suppose they want to run a long, heavy ingest on a 128 MB machine).
I do recognize that there’s possibly an issue here. But I think this issue is only a symptom, and specific effort should be planned to get rid of the underlying problem.

In parallel to any performance-tuning efforts, it might be a good idea for the customer (or the Fedora developers) to profile the application before selecting (or recommending) a particular hardware, JVM, memory heap setting. It’s not a consumer application, after all.
I believe your analysis is correct,
. I would add that if anyone runs into this issue in the future, debugging and tuning can be facilitated by adding the following JAVA_OPTS, then reproducing the error.
JAVA_OPTS="${JAVA_OPTS} -Xloggc:/tmp/java-gc.log -XX:+PrintGCDetails -XX:+PrintGCDateStamps"
The "java-gc.log" (or whatever you wish to name it) will contain memory management details that can be easily visualized with:
https://github.com/chewiebug/GCViewer
Hi there,
I am still experiencing this problem. The application fails after about 1000 ingests.
What I am missing from this ticket is a recipe for setting my JVM options to ensure that my server runs in a normal production scenario. If there is not such recipe, I still think this is an issue.
My java settings:

/usr/lib/jvm/java-1.8.0/bin/java -Djava.awt.headless=true -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8 -server -Xms512m -Xmx2048m -XX:NewSize=256m -XX:MaxNewSize=256m -XX:MetaspaceSize=64m -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=512m -XX:+DisableExplicitGC -Xloggc:/tmp/java-gc.log -XX:+PrintGCDetails -XX:+PrintGCDateStamps -Dfcrepo.home=/data/fcrepo -Dfcrepo.modeshape.configuration=file:/etc/tomcat7/lake/repository.json -Dfcrepo.activemq.configuration=file:/etc/tomcat7/lake/activemq.xml -classpath :/usr/share/tomcat7/bin/bootstrap.jar:/usr/share/tomcat7/bin/tomcat-juli.jar:/usr/share/java/commons-daemon.jar -Dcatalina.base=/usr/share/tomcat7 -Dcatalina.home=/usr/share/tomcat7 -Djava.endorsed.dirs= -Djava.io.tmpdir=/var/cache/tomcat7/temp -Djava.util.logging.config.file=/usr/share/tomcat7/conf/logging.properties -Djava.util.logging.manager=org.apache.juli.ClassLoaderLogManager org.apache.catalina.startup.Bootstrap start
See attached GC log file.
A higher -Xmx setting (e.g., something above or around 4G) should take care of the issue you're seeing.
Id did not unfortunately. Tried 4096m and 6144m and it keeps quitting between ingest #1020 and #1030. Find new GC log attached.
Increasing metaspace size to 1024m did not help either.
Some more information:
I am ingesting RDF data only, about 30 triples per resource (user-provided, not counting the server-managed ones)
My test server has 8Gb of RAM and has a few servers running. Java is taking 10Gb of virtual memory with the above settings. This is my 'top' command output

Tasks: 167 total,   1 running, 166 sleeping,   0 stopped,   0 zombie
Cpu(s):  0.6%us,  1.8%sy,  0.0%ni, 97.6%id,  0.0%wa,  0.0%hi,  0.0%si,  0.0%st
Mem:   8062472k total,  7914920k used,   147552k free,  1192864k buffers
Swap:        0k total,        0k used,        0k free,  4571976k cached

1  PID USER      PR  NI  VIRT  RES  SHR S %CPU %MEM    TIME+  COMMAND                                                                                         
  1825 tomcat    20   0 10.5g 692m  60m S 32.9  8.8   5:23.56 java
Is system memory becoming a bottleneck here?

It does appear that the system memory is not sufficient. How much memory is getting consumed by other Java applications on this machine? If it's a dev machine, one way to find out would be to download an application like JConsole – it would auto-detect and connect to applications (like Fedora) and tell you the actual statistics. There's also the GCViewer tool (that Andrew recommends).
I have two separate instances of Java running Blazegraph (the Fedora index) and Tomcat running Fedora only. These are the top ranking processes in terms of memory usage:
What do you suggest to tweak? 8Gb does not seem a low entry point for a test server to me.

I can try JConsole but the Java servers on my test machine are proxied through Apache httpd, so I have to check how to do that. I also gave GCViewer a try earlier, but for some reason it is not starting on my local machine. I will keep you posted if I can gather more information.

The reason is that although the memory you are passing it exceeds the physical memory on the machine, it's going to write the memory pages to disk, causing performance issues and ultimately OOM warnings. From the output, it's not clear to me if the other process is consuming 10.5 or 6.5 GB of virtual memory. It seems like this process could be preventing F4 from the 3-4 GB it needs (for a certain duration of time at least).
Thanks. I will try to shut down and move out other applications to see if it improves the situation and report back.

When we resolve this, I think there are two things we need to establish and document in the Fedora Wiki: 1) minimal system requirements for production and test environment; 2) recommended JVM settings (the ones in
https://wiki.duraspace.org/x/jQsCB
don't work). This will greatly help implementers getting started.
I moved to a staging server with 8Gb of RAM and only Tomcat + Fedora running. Using the following settings:
-server -Djava.awt.headless=true -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8 -Xms512m -Xmx6144m -XX:NewSize=256m -XX:MaxNewSize=256m -XX:MetaspaceSize=64m -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=1024m -XX:+DisableExplicitGC
I was able to chug through hundreds of thousands of record without a OOME. Yay!
Reiterating my previous message, I think it is important to let users know about this limitation.
As time permits, as

suggests, it would be good to investigate and limit the heap memory build up. The fact that you either need a lot of RAM or you have to restart the server after n ingests may not sound very appealing to evaluators.

When ingesting object metadata as RDF/XML, initial batches of 1000 objects are successful and pretty constant in processing time.  After 5-8 batches are loaded, the processing time increases and eventually there is the error "java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: GC overhead limit exceeded".
If I restart the servlet container between batches, the error goes away.
